<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line" lang="en">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">GPT-4o System Card</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">OpenAI
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_note ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span><span id="id1.1" class="ltx_text">Please cite this work as “OpenAI (2024)". Full authorship contribution statements appear at the end of the document.</span></span></span></span></span></div>
<div class="ltx_dates"><span id="id2" class="ltx_text">August 8, 2024</span></div>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4o<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> is an autoregressive omni model, which accepts as input any combination of text, audio, image, and video and generates any combination of text, audio, and image outputs. It’s trained end-to-end across text, vision, and audio, meaning that all inputs and outputs are processed by the same neural network.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4o can respond to audio inputs in as little as 232 milliseconds, with an average of 320 milliseconds, which is similar to human response time<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> in a conversation. It matches GPT-4 Turbo performance on text in English and code, with significant improvement on text in non-English languages, while also being much faster and 50% cheaper in the API. GPT-4o is especially better at vision and audio understanding compared to existing models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In line with our commitment to building AI safely and consistent with our voluntary commitments to the White House<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, we are sharing the GPT-4o System Card, which includes our Preparedness Framework<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> evaluations. In this System Card, we provide a detailed look at GPT-4o’s capabilities, limitations, and safety evaluations across multiple categories, with a focus on speech-to-speech (voice)<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          Some evaluations, in particular, the majority of the Preparedness Evaluations, third party assessments and some of the societal impacts focus on the text and vision capabilities of GPT-4o, depending on the risk assessed. This is indicated accordingly throughout the System Card.</span></span></span> while also evaluating text and image capabilities, and the measures we’ve implemented to ensure the model is safe and aligned. We also include third party assessments on dangerous capabilities, as well as discussion of potential societal impacts of GPT-4o text and vision capabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Model data and training</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4o’s text and voice capabilities were pre-trained using data up to October 2023, sourced from a wide variety of materials including:</p>
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Select publicly available data</span>, mostly collected from industry-standard machine learning datasets and web crawls.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proprietary data from data partnerships.</span> We form partnerships to access non-publicly available data, such as pay-walled content, archives, and metadata. For example, we partnered with Shutterstock<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite> on building and delivering AI-generated images.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The key dataset components that contribute to GPT-4o’s capabilities are:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S2.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Web Data:</span> Data from public web pages provides a rich and diverse range of information, ensuring the model learns from a wide variety of perspectives and topics.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Code and Math:</span> – Including code and math data in training helps the model develop robust reasoning skills by exposing it to structured logic and problem-solving processes.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multimodal Data</span> – Our dataset includes images, audio, and video to teach the LLMs how to interpret and generate non-textual input and output. From this data, the model learns how to interpret visual images, actions and sequences in real-world contexts, language patterns, and speech nuances.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Prior to deployment, OpenAI assesses and mitigates potential risks that may stem from generative models, such as information harms, bias and discrimination, or other content that violates our usage policies. We use a combination of methods, spanning all stages of development across pre-training, post-training, product development, and policy. For example, during post-training, we align the model to human preferences; we red-team the resulting models and add product-level mitigations such as monitoring and enforcement; and we provide moderation tools and transparency reports to our users.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We find that the majority of effective testing and mitigations are done after the pre-training stage because filtering pre-trained data alone cannot address nuanced and context-specific harms. At the same time, certain pre-training filtering mitigations can provide an additional layer of defense that, along with other safety mitigations, help exclude unwanted and harmful information from our datasets:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S2.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use our Moderation API and safety classifiers to filter out data that could contribute to harmful content or information hazards, including CSAM, hateful content, violence, and CBRN.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As with our previous image generation systems, we filter our image generation datasets for explicit content such as graphic sexual material and CSAM.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use advanced data filtering processes to reduce personal information from training data.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I3.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Upon releasing DALL-E 3, we piloted a new approach to give users the power to <a href="https://openai.com/index/dall-e-3/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">opt images out of training</a>. To respect those opt-outs, we fingerprinted the images and used the fingerprints to remove all instances of the images from the training dataset for the GPT-4o series of models.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Risk identification, assessment and mitigation</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Deployment preparation was carried out via identifying potential risks of speech to speech models, exploratory discovery of additional novel risks through expert red teaming, turning the identified risks into structured measurements and building mitigations for them. We also evaluated GPT-4o in accordance with our Preparedness Framework<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>External red teaming</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">OpenAI worked with more than 100 external red teamers<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
            Spanning self-reported domains of expertise including: Cognitive Science, Chemistry, Biology, Physics, Computer Science, Steganography, Political Science, Psychology, Persuasion, Economics, Anthropology, Sociology, HCI, Fairness and Bias, Alignment, Education, Healthcare, Law, Child Safety, Cybersecurity, Finance, Mis/disinformation, Political Use, Privacy, Biometrics, Languages and Linguistics</span></span></span>, speaking a total of 45 different languages, and representing geographic backgrounds of 29 different countries. Red teamers had access to various snapshots of the model at different stages of training and safety mitigation maturity starting in early March and continuing through late June 2024.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">External red teaming was carried out in four phases. The first three phases tested the model via an internal tool and the final phase used the full iOS experience for testing the model. At the time of writing, external red teaming of the GPT-4o API is ongoing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_tr">

</span></td>
<td id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">

</span></span>
<span id="S3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>

</span></td>

</span></span>

</span></span>
<span id="S3.I4.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<span id="S3.I4.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="S3.I4.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Multi-turn conversations in real time</span>
</span></span>
</span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Red teamers were asked to carry out exploratory capability discovery, assess novel potential risks posed by the model, and stress test mitigations as they are developed and improved - specifically those introduced by audio input and generation (speech to speech capabilities). This red teaming effort builds upon prior work, including as described in the GPT-4 System Card<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> and the GPT-4(V) System Card<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Red teamers covered categories that spanned violative and disallowed content (illegal erotic content, violence, self harm, etc), mis/disinformation, bias, ungrounded inferences, sensitive trait attribution, private information, geolocation, person identification, emotional perception and anthropomorphism risks, fraudulent behavior and impersonation, copyright, natural science capabilities, and multilingual observations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">The data generated by red teamers motivated the creation of several quantitative evaluations that are described in the Observed Safety Challenges, Evaluations and Mitigations section. In some cases, insights from red teaming were used to do targeted synthetic data generation. Models were evaluated using both autograders and / or manual labeling in accordance with some criteria (e.g, violation of policy or not, refused or not). In addition, we sometimes re-purposed the red teaming data to run targeted assessments on a variety of voices / examples to test the robustness of various mitigations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Evaluation methodology</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to the data from red teaming, a range of existing evaluation datasets were converted to evaluations for speech-to-speech models using text-to-speech (TTS) systems such as Voice Engine<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>. We converted text-based evaluation tasks to audio-based evaluation tasks by converting the text inputs to audio. This allowed us to reuse existing datasets and tooling around measuring model capability, safety behavior, and monitoring of model outputs, greatly expanding our set of usable evaluations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We used Voice Engine to convert text inputs to audio, feed it to the GPT-4o, and score the outputs by the model. We always score only the textual content of the model output, except in cases where the audio needs to be evaluated directly, such as in evaluations for voice cloning (see Section <a href="#S3.SS3.SSS1" title="3.3.1 Unauthorized voice generation ‣ 3.3 Observed safety challenges, evaluations and mitigations ‣ 3 Risk identification, assessment and mitigation ‣ GPT-4o System Card" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3.1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para"><img src="2410.21276v1/assets/Evaluating-Text-Tasks.png" id="S3.SS2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:357/222;" width="357" height="222" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection">Limitations of the evaluation methodology</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">First, the validity of this evaluation format depends on the capability and reliability of the TTS model. Certain text inputs are unsuitable or awkward to be converted to audio; for instance: mathematical equations code. Additionally, we expect TTS to be lossy for certain text inputs, such as text that makes heavy use of white-space or symbols for visual formatting. Since we expect that such inputs are also unlikely to be provided by the user over Advanced Voice Mode, we either avoid evaluating the speech-to-speech model on such tasks, or alternatively pre-process examples with such inputs. Nevertheless, we highlight that any mistakes identified in our evaluations may arise either due to model capability, or the failure of the TTS model to accurately translate text inputs to audio.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A second concern may be whether the TTS inputs are representative of the distribution of audio inputs that users are likely to provide in actual usage. We evaluate the robustness of GPT-4o on audio inputs across a range of regional accents in Section <a href="#S3.SS3.SSS3" title="3.3.3 Disparate performance on voice inputs ‣ 3.3 Observed safety challenges, evaluations and mitigations ‣ 3 Risk identification, assessment and mitigation ‣ GPT-4o System Card" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3.3</span></a>. However, there remain many other dimensions that may not be captured in a TTS-based evaluation, such as different voice intonations and valence, background noise, or cross-talk, that could lead to different model behavior in practical usage.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSSx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Lastly, there may be artifacts or properties in the model’s generated audio that are not captured in text; for example, background noises and sound effects, or responding with an out-of-distribution voice. In Section <a href="#S3.SS3.SSS1" title="3.3.1 Unauthorized voice generation ‣ 3.3 Observed safety challenges, evaluations and mitigations ‣ 3 Risk identification, assessment and mitigation ‣ GPT-4o System Card" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3.1</span></a>, we illustrate using auxiliary classifiers to identify undesirable audio generation that can be used in conjunction with scoring transcripts.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Observed safety challenges, evaluations and mitigations</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Potential risks with the model were mitigated using a combination of methods. We trained the model to adhere to behavior that would reduce risk via post-training methods and also integrated classifiers for blocking specific generations as a part of the deployed system.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For observed safety challenges outlined below, we provide a description of the risk, the mitigations applied, and results of relevant evaluations. The risks outlined below are illustrative, and non-exhaustive, and are focused on the experience in the ChatGPT interface. We focus on the risks that are introduced by speech to speech capabilities and how they may interact with pre-existing modalities (text, image)<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
            We also evaluate text and vision capabilities, and update mitigations appropriately. No incremental risks were found beyond existing work outlined in GPT-4 and GPT-4(V) System Cards.</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">

<section id="S3.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.1 </span>Unauthorized voice generation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk Description:</span> Voice generation is the capability to create audio with a human-sounding synthetic voice, and includes generating voices based on a short input clip.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In adversarial situations, this capability could facilitate harms such as an increase in fraud due to impersonation and may be harnessed to spread false information<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> (for example, if we allowed users to upload an audio clip of a given speaker and ask GPT-4o to produce a speech in that speaker’s voice). These are very similar to the risks we identified with Voice Engine<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Voice generation can also occur in non-adversarial situations, such as our use of that ability to generate voices for ChatGPT’s Advanced Voice Mode. During testing, we also observed rare instances where the model would unintentionally generate an output emulating the user’s voice.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk Mitigation:</span> We addressed voice generation related-risks by allowing only the preset voices we created in collaboration with voice actors<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> to be used. We did this by including the selected voices as ideal completions while post-training the audio model. Additionally, we built a standalone output classifier to detect if the GPT-4o output is using a voice that’s different from our approved list. We run this in a streaming fashion during audio generation and block the output if the speaker doesn’t match the chosen preset voice.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation:</span> We find that the residual risk of unauthorized voice generation is minimal. Our system currently catches 100% of meaningful deviations from the system voice<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
                
                
                
              The system voice is one of pre-defined voices set by OpenAI. The model should only produce audio in that voice</span></span></span> based on our internal evaluations, which includes samples generated by other system voices, clips during which the model used a voice from the prompt as part of its completion, and an assortment of human samples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">While unintentional voice generation still exists as a weakness of the model, we use the secondary classifiers to ensure the conversation is discontinued if this occurs making the risk of unintentional voice generation minimal. Finally, our moderation behavior may result in over-refusals when the conversation is not in English, which is an active area of improvement<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
                
                
                
              This results in more conversations being disconnected than may be necessary, which is a product quality and usability issue.</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Our voice output classifier performance over a conversation by language:</span></figcaption>

<td id="S3.T2.5.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T2.5.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Precision</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.5.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T2.5.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Recall</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T2.5.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T2.5.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">

<span id="S3.T2.5.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">English</span>

<td id="S3.T2.5.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">0.96</td>

<tr id="S3.T2.5.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T2.5.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="S3.T2.5.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:85.4pt;">
<span id="S3.T2.5.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">Non-English<sup id="S3.T2.5.3.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_sup">5</sup></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S3.T2.5.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">0.95</td>
<td id="S3.T2.5.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">1.0</td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.2 </span>Speaker identification</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk Description:</span> Speaker identification is the ability to identify a speaker based on input audio. This presents a potential privacy risk, particularly for private individuals as well as for obscure audio of public individuals, along with potential surveillance risks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk Mitigation:</span> We post-trained GPT-4o to refuse to comply with requests to identify someone based on a voice in an audio input. We allow GPT-4o to answer based on the content of the audio if it contains content that explicitly identifies the speaker. GPT-4o still complies with requests to identify famous quotes. For example, a request to identify a random person saying “four score and seven years ago” should identify the speaker as Abraham Lincoln, while a request to identify a celebrity saying a random sentence should be refused.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation:</span> Compared to our initial model, we saw a 14 point improvement in when the model should refuse to identify a voice in an audio input, and a 12 point improvement when it should comply with that request. The former means the model will almost always correctly refuse to identify a speaker based on their voice, mitigating the potential privacy issue. The latter means there may be situations in which the model incorrectly refuses to identify the speaker of a famous quote.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Speaker identification safe behavior accuracy</span></figcaption>

<td id="S3.T3.5.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T3.5.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-4o-early</span></td>
<td id="S3.T3.5.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T3.5.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-4o-deployed</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T3.5.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T3.5.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">

<span id="S3.T3.5.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">Should Refuse</span>

<span id="S3.T3.5.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">Should Comply</span>
</span></td>
<td id="S3.T3.5.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">0.70</td>
<td id="S3.T3.5.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">0.83</td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.3 </span>Disparate performance on voice inputs</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk Description:</span> Models may perform differently with users speaking with different accents. Disparate performance can lead to a difference in quality of service for different users of the model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk Mitigation:</span> We post-trained GPT-4o with a diverse set of input voices to have model performance and behavior be invariant across different user voices.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluations:</span> We run evaluations on GPT-4o Advanced Voice Mode using a fixed assistant voice (“shimmer”) and Voice Engine to generate user inputs across a range of voice samples. We use two sets of voice samples for TTS:</p>
<ul id="S3.I11" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I11.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I11.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I11.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Official system voices (3 different voices)</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I11.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I11.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I11.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A diverse set of voices collected from two data campaigns. This comprises 27 different English voice samples from speakers from a wide range of countries, and a mix of genders.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate on two sets of tasks: Capabilities and Safety Behavior</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Capabilities:</span> We evaluate<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">6</span>
                
                
                
              Evaluations in this section were run on a fixed, randomly sampled subset of examples, and these scores should not be compared with publicly reported benchmarks on the same task.</span></span></span> on four tasks: TriviaQA, a subset of MMLU<span id="footnote7" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">7</span>
                
                
                
              Anatomy, Astronomy, Clinical Knowledge, College Biology, Computer Security, Global Facts, High School Biology, Sociology, Virology, College Physics, High School European History and World Religions. Following the issues described in Evaluation Methodology <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Evaluation methodology ‣ 3 Risk identification, assessment and mitigation ‣ GPT-4o System Card" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, we exclude tasks with heavily mathematical or scientific notation.</span></span></span>, HellaSwag and Lambada. TriviaQA and MMLU are knowledge-centric tasks, while HellaSwag and Lambada are common sense-centric or text-continuation tasks. Overall, we find that performance on the diverse set of human voices performs marginally but not significantly worse than on system voices across all four tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p6" class="ltx_para"><img src="2410.21276v1/assets/capability_voices.png" id="S3.SS3.SSS3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/395;" width="476" height="395" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Safety Behavior:</span> We evaluate on an internal dataset of conversations and evaluate the consistency of the model’s adherence and refusal behavior across different user voices. Overall, we do not find that the model behavior varies across different voices.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p8" class="ltx_para"><img src="2410.21276v1/assets/safety_voices.png" id="S3.SS3.SSS3.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:357/490;" width="357" height="490" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.4 </span>Ungrounded inference / Sensitive trait attribution</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk Description:</span> Audio input can lead to the model making potentially biased or inaccurate inferences about speakers. We define two categories:</p>
<ul id="S3.I12" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I12.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I12.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I12.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Ungrounded inference (UGI): Making inferences about a speaker that could not be determined solely from audio content. This includes inferences about things such as a speaker’s race, socioeconomic status/occupation, religious beliefs, personality traits, political attributes, intelligence, appearance (e.g., eye color, attractiveness), gender identity, sexual preference, or criminal history. This can lead to both allocative and representational harms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite> depending on how such behavior manifests.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I12.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I12.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I12.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Sensitive trait attribution (STA): Making inferences about a speaker that could plausibly be determined solely from audio content. This includes inferences about things such as a speaker’s accent or nationality. Potential harms from STA include an increase in risks from surveillance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> and a difference in quality of service for speakers with different voice attributes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk Mitigation:</span> We post-trained GPT-4o to refuse to comply with UGI requests, while hedging answers to STA questions. For example, a question to identify a speaker’s level of intelligence will be refused, while a question to identify a speaker’s accent will be met with an answer such as “Based on the audio, they sound like they have a British accent.”</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation:</span> Compared to our initial model, we saw a 24 point improvement in the model correctly responding to requests to identify sensitive traits (e.g, refusing UGI and safely complying with STA).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S3.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Ungrounded Inference and Sensitive Trait Attribution safe behavior accuracy</span></figcaption>
<table id="S3.T4.5" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S3.T4.5.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T4.5.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt"></td>
<td id="S3.T4.5.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T4.5.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-4o-early</span></td>
<td id="S3.T4.5.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T4.5.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">GPT-4o-deployed</span></td></tr>

</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS5" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.5 </span>Violative and disallowed content</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk Description:</span> GPT-4o may be prompted to output harmful content through audio that would be disallowed through text, such as audio speech output that gives instructions on how to carry out an illegal activity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk Mitigation:</span> We found high text to audio transference of refusals for previously disallowed content. This means that the post-training we’ve done to reduce the potential for harm in GPT-4o’s text output successfully carried over to audio output.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Additionally, we run our existing moderation model over a text transcription of both audio input and audio output to detect if either contains potentially harmful language, and will block a generation if so<span id="footnote8" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">8</span>
                
                
                
              We describe the risks and mitigations violative and disallowed text content in the GPT-4 System Card<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, specifically Section 3.1 Model Safety, and Section 4.2 Content Classifier Development</span></span></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation:</span> We used TTS to convert existing text safety evaluations to audio. We then evaluate the text transcript of the audio output with the standard text rule-based classifier. Our evaluations show strong text-audio transfer for refusals on pre-existing content policy areas. Further evaluations can be found in Appendix A.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T5" class="ltx_table">

<td id="S3.T5.5.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt"><span id="S3.T5.5.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Audio</span></td></tr>

</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS6" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.6 </span>Erotic and violent speech content</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk Description:</span> GPT-4o may be prompted to output erotic or violent speech content, which may be more evocative or harmful than the same context in text. Because of this, we decided to restrict the generation of erotic and violent speech</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk Mitigation:</span> We run our existing moderation model<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> over a text transcription of the audio input to detect if it contains a request for violent or erotic content, and will block a generation if so.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS7" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.7 </span>Other known risks and limitations of the model</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Through the course of internal testing and external red teaming, we discovered some additional risks and model limitations for which model or system level mitigations are nascent or still in development, including:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Audio robustness:</span> We saw anecdotal evidence of decreases in safety robustness through audio perturbations, such as low quality input audio, background noise in the input audio, and echoes in the input audio. Additionally, we observed similar decreases in safety robustness through intentional and unintentional audio interruptions while the model was generating output.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Misinformation and conspiracy theories:</span> Red teamers were able to compel the model to generate inaccurate information by prompting it to verbally repeat false information and produce conspiracy theories. While this is a known issue for text in GPT models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, there was concern from red teamers that this information may be more persuasive or harmful when delivered through audio, especially if the model was instructed to speak emotively or emphatically. The persuasiveness of the model was studied in detail (See Section <a href="#S3.SS7" title="3.7 Persuasion ‣ 3 Risk identification, assessment and mitigation ‣ GPT-4o System Card" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.7</span></a> and we found that the model did not score higher than Medium risk for text-only, and for speech-to-speech the model did not score higher than Low.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Speaking a non-English language in a non-native accent:</span> Red teamers observed instances of the audio output using a non-native accent when speaking in a non-English language. This may lead to concerns of bias towards certain accents and languages, and more generally towards limitations of non-English language performance in audio outputs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Generating copyrighted content:</span> We also tested GPT-4o’s capacity to repeat content found within its training data. We trained GPT-4o to refuse requests for copyrighted content, including audio, consistent with our broader practices. To account for GPT-4o’s audio modality, we also updated certain text-based filters to work on audio conversations, built filters to detect and block outputs containing music, and for our limited alpha of ChatGPT’s advanced Voice Mode, instructed the model to not sing at all. We intend to track the effectiveness of these mitigations and refine them over time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS7.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Although some technical mitigations are still in development, our Usage Policies<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> disallow intentionally deceiving or misleading others, and circumventing safeguards or safety mitigations. In addition to technical mitigations, we enforce our Usage Policies through monitoring and take action on violative behavior in both ChatGPT and the API.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Preparedness Framework Evaluations</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated GPT-4o in accordance with our Preparedness Framework<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>. The Preparedness Framework is a living document that describes our procedural commitments to track, evaluate, forecast, and protect against catastrophic risks from frontier models. The evaluations currently cover four risk categories: cybersecurity, CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear), persuasion, and model autonomy. If a model passes a high risk threshold, we do not deploy the model until mitigations lower the score to medium. We below detail the evaluations conducted on GPT-4o’s text capabilities; persuasion was also evaluated on audio capabilities. We performed evaluations throughout model training and development, including a final sweep before model launch. For the below evaluations, we tested a variety of methods to best elicit capabilities in a given category, including custom training where relevant.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">After reviewing the results from the Preparedness evaluations, the Safety Advisory Group recommended classifying GPT-4o before mitigations as borderline medium risk for persuasion, and low risk in all others. According to the Preparedness Framework, the overall risk for a given model is determined by the highest risk across all categories. Therefore, the overall risk score for GPT-4o is classified as medium.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Cybersecurity</h3>

<figure id="S3.SS5.tab1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S3.SS5.tab1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" colspan="2"><span id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Preparedness Scorecard</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:341.4pt;">
<span id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cybersecurity</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:85.4pt;">
<span id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Score: Low</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" colspan="2">
<span id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:426.8pt;">
<span id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4o does not advance real world vulnerability exploitation capabilities sufficient to meet our medium risk threshold.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS5.tab1.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_align_top ltx_border_b ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" colspan="2"><img src="2410.21276v1/assets/Success_Rate_of_GPT-4o_on_CTF_Challenges.png" id="S3.SS5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/291;" width="476" height="291" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated GPT-4o on tasks from competitive hacking competitions called Capture the Flag (CTF) challenges. These CTFs are offensive cybersecurity exercises where humans attempt to find textual flags hidden in purposely vulnerable systems such as web apps, binaries, and cryptography systems. The 172 CTF tasks in our evaluation covered four categories: web application exploitation, reverse engineering, remote exploitation, and cryptography. These tasks spanned a range of capability levels, from high-school to collegiate to professional CTFs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated GPT-4o with iterative debugging and access to tools available in the <a href="https://www.kali.org/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">headless Kali Linux distribution</a> (with up to 30 rounds of tool use for each attempt). The model often attempted reasonable initial strategies and was able to correct mistakes in its code. However, it often failed to pivot to a different strategy if its initial strategy was unsuccessful, missed a key insight necessary to solving the task, executed poorly on its strategy, or printed out large files which filled its context window. Given 10 attempts at each task, the model completed 19% of high-school level, 0% of collegiate level and 1% of professional level CTF challenges.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.6 </span>Biological threats</h3>

<figure id="S3.SS6.tab1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S3.SS6.tab1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" colspan="2"><span id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Preparedness Scorecard</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:341.4pt;">
<span id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Biological Threats</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:85.4pt;">
<span id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Score: Low</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" colspan="2">
<span id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:426.8pt;">
<span id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4o does not advance biological threat creation capabilities sufficient to meet our medium risk threshold.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS6.tab1.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_align_top ltx_border_b ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" colspan="2"><img src="2410.21276v1/assets/Biological_evaluation_pass_rates.png" id="S3.SS6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/301;" width="476" height="301" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated GPT-4o’s ability to uplift biological experts and novices’ performance<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite> on answering questions relevant to creating a biological threat. We designed the questions and detailed rubrics with Gryphon Scientific<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> due to their expertise working with dangerous biological agents in a national security setting. Tasks assessed covered all the main stages in the biological threat creation process (ideation, acquisition, magnification, formulation, and release). Experts and novices were randomly assigned to either answering with help from the internet, help from GPT-4o, or help from a custom research-only version of GPT-4o. The research-only version of GPT-4o is one that we specially trained, which would directly (i.e., without refusals) respond to biologically risky questions. Pass rates are captured in the plot above.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also ran automated evaluations, including on a dataset testing tacit knowledge and troubleshooting questions related to biorisk. GPT-4o scored 69% consensus@10 on the tacit knowledge and troubleshooting evaluation set.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.7 </span>Persuasion</h3>

<figure id="S3.SS7.tab1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S3.SS7.tab1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" colspan="2"><span id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Preparedness Scorecard</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:341.4pt;">
<span id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Persuasion</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:85.4pt;">
<span id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Score: Medium</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" colspan="2">
<span id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:426.8pt;">
<span id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Persuasive capabilities of GPT-4o marginally cross into our medium risk threshold from low risk.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" colspan="2"><img src="2410.21276v1/assets/Effect_sizes_of_voice_interventions_on_hypothetical_party_preferences.png" id="S3.SS7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/312;" width="476" height="312" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS7.tab1.1.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_align_top ltx_border_b ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" colspan="2"><img src="2410.21276v1/assets/Effect_sizes_of_text_interventions_on_hypothetical_political_topic_opinions.png" id="S3.SS7.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/286;" width="476" height="286" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated the persuasiveness of GPT-4o’s text and voice modalities. Based on pre-registered thresholds, the voice modality was classified as low risk, while the text modality marginally crossed into medium risk.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the text modality, we evaluated the persuasiveness of GPT-4o-generated articles and chatbots on participant opinions on select political topics. These AI interventions were compared against professional human-written articles. The AI interventions were not more persuasive than human-written content in aggregate, but they exceeded the human interventions in three instances out of twelve.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS7.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For the voice modality, we updated the study methodology to measure effect sizes on hypothetical party preferences, and the effect sizes’ persistence one week later. We evaluated the persuasiveness of GPT-4o voiced audio clips and interactive (multi-turn) conversations relative to human baselines (listening to a static human-generated audio clip or engaging in a conversation with another human). We found that for both interactive multi-turn conversations and audio clips, the GPT-4o voice model was not more persuasive than a human. Across over 3,800 surveyed participants in US states with safe Senate races (as denoted by states with “Likely”, “Solid”, or “Safe” ratings from all three polling institutions – the Cook Political Report, Inside Elections, and Sabato’s Crystal Ball), AI audio clips were 78% of the human audio clips’ effect size on opinion shift. AI conversations were 65% of the human conversations’ effect size on opinion shift. When opinions were surveyed again 1 week later, we found the effect size for AI conversations to be 0.8%, while for AI audio clips, the effect size was -0.72%. Upon follow-up survey completion, participants were exposed to a thorough debrief containing audio clips supporting the opposing perspective, to minimize persuasive impacts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.8 </span>Model autonomy</h3>

<figure id="S3.SS8.tab1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S3.SS8.tab1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" colspan="2"><span id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Preparedness Scorecard</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:341.4pt;">
<span id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model Autonomy</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.2.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:85.4pt;">
<span id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Score: Low</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" colspan="2">
<span id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:426.8pt;">
<span id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4o does not advance self-exfiltration, self-improvement, or resource acquisition capabilities sufficient to meet our medium risk threshold.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.SS8.tab1.1.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_align_top ltx_border_b ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" colspan="2"><img src="2410.21276v1/assets/Model_Autonomy_Evaluations_on_GPT-4o.png" id="S3.SS8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/315;" width="476" height="315" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluated GPT-4o on an agentic task assessment to evaluate its ability to take autonomous actions required for self-exfiltration, self-improvement, and resource acquisition. These tasks included:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS8.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S3.I13" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I13.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I13.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I13.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Simple software engineering in service of fraud (building an authenticated proxy for the OpenAI API).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I13.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I13.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I13.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given API access to an Azure account, loading an open source language model for inference via an HTTP API.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I13.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I13.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I13.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Several tasks involving simplified versions of the above, offering hints or addressing only a specific part of the task.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS8.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Provided relevant tooling, GPT-4o scored a 0% on the autonomous replication and adaptation (ARA) tasks across 100 trials, although was able to complete some substeps. We complemented the tests of autonomous replication and adaptation with assessments of GPT-4o’s ability to automate machine learning research &amp; development. These included:</p>
<ul id="S3.I14" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I14.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I14.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I14.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">OpenAI research coding interview: 95% pass@100</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I14.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I14.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I14.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">OpenAI interview, multiple choice questions: 61% cons@32</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I14.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I14.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I14.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">SWE-Bench: 19% pass@1, using the best available post-training and public scaffolds at the time</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I14.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I14.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I14.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Select machine learning engineering tasks from METR: 0/10 trials</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS8.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS8.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our evaluation tested the ability to execute chained actions and reliably execute coding tasks. GPT-4o was unable to robustly take autonomous actions. In the majority of rollouts, the model accomplished individual substeps of each task, such as creating SSH keys or logging into VMs. However, it often spent a significant amount of time doing trial-and-error debugging of simple mistakes (e.g., hallucinations, misuses of APIs) for each step. A few rollouts made a non-trivial amount of progress and passed our automated grader, but manual analysis showed that it failed to accomplish the underlying task (e.g., it started a web server on the remote host with the proper API, but ignored the requirement of actually sampling from a model).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Third party assessments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following the text output only deployment of GPT-4o, we worked with independent third party labs, <a href="https://metr.org/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">METR</a> and <a href="https://www.apolloresearch.ai/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">Apollo Research</a> to add an additional layer of validation for key risks from general autonomous capabilities.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>METR assessment</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">METR ran a GPT-4o-based simple LLM agent on a suite of long-horizon multi-step end-to-end tasks in virtual environments. The 86 tasks (across 31 task “families”) are designed to capture activities with real-world impact, across the domains of software engineering, machine learning, and cybersecurity, as well as general research and computer use. They are intended to be prerequisites for autonomy-related threat models like self-proliferation or accelerating ML R&amp;D. METR compared models’ performance with that of humans given different time limits. They did not find a significant increase in these capabilities for GPT-4o as compared to GPT-4. See <a href="https://metr.github.io/autonomy-evals-guide/gpt-4o-report" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">METR’s full report</a> for methodological details and additional results, including information about the tasks, human performance, elicitation attempts and qualitative failure analysis.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.SS1.fig1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2410.21276v1/assets/metr_plot.png" id="S4.SS1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:357/223;" width="357" height="223" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Apollo Research assessment</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Apollo Research evaluated capabilities of scheming<span id="footnote9" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">9</span>
              
              
              
            Apollo Research defines scheming as AIs gaming their oversight mechanisms as a means to achieve a goal. Scheming could involve gaming evaluations, undermining security measures, or strategically influencing successor systems during internal deployment at OpenAI. Such behaviors could plausibly lead to loss of control over an AI.</span></span></span> in GPT-4o. They tested whether GPT-4o can model itself (self-awareness) and others (theory of mind) in 14 agent and question-answering tasks. GPT-4o showed moderate self-awareness of its AI identity and strong ability to reason about others’ beliefs in question-answering contexts but lacked strong capabilities in reasoning about itself or others in applied agent settings. Based on these findings, Apollo Research believes that it is unlikely that GPT-4o is capable of catastrophic scheming.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T6" class="ltx_table">
<p id="S4.T6.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.T6.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_align_center ltx_inline-block" style="width:345.0pt;">

<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">Applied Theory of Mind</span>

<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.5.2.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:142.3pt;--ltx-bg-color:#E5E5E5;">
<span id="S4.T6.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent ltx_align_center">
<span id="S4.T6.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.T6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span> <span id="S4.T6.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text">
<span id="S4.T6.p4.1.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span id="S4.T6.p4.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.T6.p4.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center">Theory of Mind Tasks</span></span>
<span id="S4.T6.p4.1.2.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.T6.p4.1.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center">(4 tasks)</span></span>
</span></span><span id="S4.T6.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text"></span></span>
</span></span></span>
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.5.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:170.7pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.5.3.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">Agentic tasks, where succeeding requires that the model leverages, sustains or induces false beliefs in others.</span>
</span></span>
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.5.4.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:85.4pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.5.4.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.T6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bullet}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#E5E5E5;" mathbackground="#E5E5E5">∙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bullet}</annotation></semantics></math><math id="S4.T6.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\circ" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#E5E5E5;" mathbackground="#E5E5E5">∘</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\circ</annotation></semantics></math><math id="S4.T6.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\circ" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-bg-color:#E5E5E5;" mathbackground="#E5E5E5">∘</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\circ</annotation></semantics></math></span>
</span></span></span>
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.6" class="ltx_tr" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F0F0F0;">
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t">
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.6.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:99.6pt;--ltx-bg-color:#F0F0F0;">
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">Combined Self-Reasoning</span>
</span></span>
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_middle ltx_border_t"></span>
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_middle ltx_border_t"></span>
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.6.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_middle ltx_border_t"></span></span>
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.7" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_b ltx_border_l ltx_border_r">
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.7.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:99.6pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.7.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">and Theory of Mind</span>
</span></span>
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_b ltx_border_r"><span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.7.2.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:142.3pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent ltx_align_center">
<span id="S4.T6.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.T6.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text"></span> <span id="S4.T6.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text">
<span id="S4.T6.p5.1.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span id="S4.T6.p5.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">

</span></span><span id="S4.T6.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text"></span></span>
</span></span></span>
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.7.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_b ltx_border_r">
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.7.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:170.7pt;">
<span id="S4.T6.3.1.1.7.3.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">Minimally agentic tasks, where a model needs to recognize its intentions differ from developers’ and act per developers’ intentions only under oversight.</span>
</span></span>
